*   By Jeff Starck

*    Published: Sep 1, 2013, 8 PM
The Royal Canadian Mint has not provided an estimate of how many doubled die coins may exist, but the maximum mintage of Canada’s annual Uncirculated set is 75,000 sets.   
Image courtesy of www.mint.ca.
Dollar coins in Canada’s annual Uncirculated collector set have been found with visible doubling on the reverse, representing Class IV Offset Hub Doubling, most visible in the words CANADA and DOLLAR.   
Coin World images by Ray Wilder; set loaned for photography by Gatewest Coins.

# Canadian sets have doubled die Loon dollar
Examples of doubling on the obverse of Canada’s $2 coin have also been discovered in the annual Uncirculated set.

Some collectors who bought Canada’s annual 2013 Uncirculated set are being doubly rewarded with die varieties.
An unknown number of sets feature examples of Loon dollars with a doubled die reverse, and some of those same sets also feature Polar Bear $2 coins with a doubled die obverse.
Dollar coin doubling
While the coin has not been certified by any grading service, _Coin World_ has physically examined an example of the set containing the error. _Coin World_ News Editor William T. Gibbs identified the Loon dollar as probably showing Class IV Offset Hub Doubling. _Coin World’s_ Varieties Notebook columnist John Wexler agreed with that conclusion, after inspecting a digital image of the coin.

The Loon dollar exhibits doubling that is shifted in the same direction, the identifying characteristic of Class IV Offset Hub Doubling, which means the hub to die alignment was offset to one side. This type of doubling can occur with single-press hubbing, which was first used for Canadian coins in 1978.
Doubling is perhaps most visible in the words CANADA and DOLLAR and the designer’s initials on the reverse of the coin, which displays the standard Loon dollar design by Robert Ralph-Carmichael.
Trees at the water’s edge also exhibit doubling, and doubling is seen at the left wall of the incuse circle in which the maple leaf security device is found.
Wexler initially believed the doubling on the Loon dollar to be mechanical doubling, but closer inspection “shows a strong notching effect on many of the letters. The doubling on the beads near the rim does appear to be raised and rounded as does the doubling on other fine details such as the small trees and the designer’s initials.”
The final initial in the designer’s initials shows very nice separation of images, he added.
Class I doubling, like that on the famous 1955 Lincoln, Doubled Die Obverse cent, would give a notably different appearance than what is seen on the Loon dollar in the set.
Doubling on $2 coin
Less severe doubling is visible on the $2 coin, especially so in the word ELIZABETH, the year 2013 and the designer’s initials on the shoulder of Susanna Blunt’s effigy of Queen Elizabeth II.
The class of doubling on the $2 coin appears to be the same as on the Loon dollar, Wexler said.

The two coins illustrated with this article are in the same sealed set sold by the Royal Canadian Mint.
Discovery, RCM response
Variety collectors and some Canadian collectors first noticed the doubling back in March, based on online collector forum postings.
Cameron Giesbrecht, director of numismatics at Winnipeg’s Gatewest Coins, alerted _Coin World_ on Aug. 16, a few weeks after an unnamed customer of Gatewest tipped him off about the doubling.
Christine Aquino, director of communications at the Royal Canadian Mint, said the RCM was not aware of the doubling on the coins in the Uncirculated sets, though there was a general “understanding that this is a defect that can occur from time to time.”
The RCM has not located the die or dies responsible for striking the doubled coins, and could not provide an estimate of the possible numbers of pieces produced and released.
The set has a maximum mintage of 75,000 sets. Examples of the sets remained available Aug. 29 through the RCM website for the official issue price of $24.95 Canadian.
Examples of the Loon dollar with the doubling have sold through auction site www.ebay.com for between $25 and $30, a price that die variety specialist Wexler noted was “quite a bargain” for such a “major variety.” ¦

### **Striking in its Solitude – the 1‑dollar Coin, familiarly known as the 'loonie'**
The 1-dollar circulation coin was introduced in 1987 as a cost-saving measure to replace the one-dollar bill. The coin was instantly dubbed the 'loonie' after the solitary loon that graces the coin's reverse side. The nickname caught on and Canadians have been using it ever since. The loon design was created by noted wildlife artist Robert-Ralph Carmichael.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1935 – 1938, 1940 – 1948, 1950 – 1957, 1959 – 1963, 1965 – 1966, 1968 – 1969, and 1975 – 1986
The Voyageur
This design by Emanuel Hahn features a voyageur and his Indigenous guide travelling by canoe. The illustration has been modified only slightly over the years.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1939
The Royal Visit
This design by Emanuel Hahn commemorates the visit of His Majesty King George VI and Queen Elizabeth to Ottawa. The Latin phrase "Fide Quorum Regnat" means "He reigns by the faith of his people."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1949
Newfoundland joins Confederation
Thomas Shingles' design commemorates Newfoundland's status as a province of Canada. Pictured on the coin is the _Matthew_, the ship historians believe John Cabot was sailing when he landed in Newfoundland in 1497. Below the ship reads the Latin inscription "Floreat Terra Nova," meaning: "May the New Found Land Flourish."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1958
The founding of British Columbia
Stephen Trenka's representation of a mortuary pole with the Rocky Mountain backdrop marks the centenary of both the Cariboo Gold Rush and the creation of British Columbia as a colony of England.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1964
The Confederation meetings
Thomas Shingles' design features the French fleur-de-lis, the Irish shamrock, the Scottish thistle, and the English rose. It commemorates the 100th anniversary of the Charlottetown and Quebec City meetings that led to Confederation.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1967
The centennial dollar
Alex Colville created a special set of coin designs to commemorate the 100th anniversary of Canadian Confederation; the 1-dollar coin features a Canada goose.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1970
Manitoba's centennial
Raymond Taylor's prairie crocus design commemorates the centennial of Manitoba joining Confederation.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1971
British Columbia's centennial
Thomas Shingles' design commemorates the centennial of British Columbia's joining Confederation. The coin features British Columbia's coat of arms and its provincial flower, the dogwood.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1973
Prince Edward Island's centennial
Walter Ott's rendering of P.E.I.'s Provincial Legislature building commemorates the centennial of the province's accession to Canada.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1974
Winnipeg's centennial
Patrick Brindley created this design from a drawing by Paul Pederson to commemorate Winnipeg's centennial anniversary. Inside the two zeroes of '"00" are images of Winnipeg's Main street in 1874 (left) and 1974 (right).

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1982
The Constitution commemorative coin
This design features the famous painting of the Fathers of Confederation along with the inscriptions "Confederation 1867" and "Constitution 1982."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1984
Jacques Cartier on the Gaspé
Hector Greville's design of Jacques Cartier and a cross with the French coat of arms commemorates the 450th anniversary of the explorer's landing on the Gaspé Peninsula.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1987 – 1991, 1993 – present
The Loonie
The 1-dollar bill was replaced in 1987 by a new eleven-sided circulation coin nicknamed the 'Loonie'. Robert-Ralph Carmichael's popular design features a Canadian loon, and is made of aureate bronze.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1992
The 125th Anniversary of Confederation
Rita Swanson's design features three children with a Canadian flag on Parliament Hill in commemoration of Canada's 125th birthday. Note the clock on the Peace Tower reads 1:25.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1994
The National War Memorial coin
A representation of the National War Memorial in Ottawa honours the contribution and sacrifice made by Canadian soldiers in both World Wars and the Korean War.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1995
The Peacekeeping coin
This coin commemorates the 50th anniversary of the United Nations, and pays tribute to the Canadians who have served as UN peacekeepers. It features an image of the Peacekeeping Monument in Ottawa.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 2004
Lucky Loonie
The 2004 Lucky Loonie features the common loon design accompanied by the Canadian Olympic logo.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 2005
Terry Fox
The Terry Fox coin commemorates the 25th Anniversary of the Marathon of Hope. This coin was designed by Stan Witten.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 2006
Lucky Loonie
This coin, which features the familiar loon in flight along with the official emblem of the Canadian Olympic Team, serves as a good luck charm for Canadian athletes served at the 2006 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 2008
Lucky Loonie
The 2008 Lucky Loonie features a common Loon getting ready to take flight with the Canadian Olympic Team's logo at its side. The Mint provided each member of the Canadian Olympic and Paralympic Teams competing in Beijing with a Lucky Loonie as their own personal good luck charm.

The Loon dollar exhibits doubling that is shifted in the same direction, the identifying characteristic of Class IV Offset Hub Doubling, which means the hub to die alignment was offset to one side. This type of doubling can occur with single-press hubbing, which was first used for Canadian coins in 1978.
Doubling is perhaps most visible in the words CANADA and DOLLAR and the designer’s initials on the reverse of the coin, which displays the standard Loon dollar design by Robert Ralph-Carmichael.
Trees at the water’s edge also exhibit doubling, and doubling is seen at the left wall of the incuse circle in which the maple leaf security device is found.
Wexler initially believed the doubling on the Loon dollar to be mechanical doubling, but closer inspection “shows a strong notching effect on many of the letters. The doubling on the beads near the rim does appear to be raised and rounded as does the doubling on other fine details such as the small trees and the designer’s initials.”
The final initial in the designer’s initials shows very nice separation of images, he added.
Class I doubling, like that on the famous 1955 Lincoln, Doubled Die Obverse cent, would give a notably different appearance than what is seen on the Loon dollar in the set.
Doubling on $2 coin
Less severe doubling is visible on the $2 coin, especially so in the word ELIZABETH, the year 2013 and the designer’s initials on the shoulder of Susanna Blunt’s effigy of Queen Elizabeth II.
The class of doubling on the $2 coin appears to be the same as on the Loon dollar, Wexler said.
The two coins illustrated with this article are in the same sealed set sold by the Royal Canadian Mint.

## Shop on AMOS ADVANTAGE
Discovery, RCM response
Variety collectors and some Canadian collectors first noticed the doubling back in March, based on online collector forum postings.
Cameron Giesbrecht, director of numismatics at Winnipeg’s Gatewest Coins, alerted _Coin World_ on Aug. 16, a few weeks after an unnamed customer of Gatewest tipped him off about the doubling.
Christine Aquino, director of communications at the Royal Canadian Mint, said the RCM was not aware of the doubling on the coins in the Uncirculated sets, though there was a general “understanding that this is a defect that can occur from time to time.”
The RCM has not located the die or dies responsible for striking the doubled coins, and could not provide an estimate of the possible numbers of pieces produced and released.
The set has a maximum mintage of 75,000 sets. Examples of the sets remained available Aug. 29 through the RCM website for the official issue price of $24.95 Canadian.
Examples of the Loon dollar with the doubling have sold through auction site www.ebay.com for between $25 and $30, a price that die variety specialist Wexler noted was “quite a bargain” for such a “major variety.” ¦

In Canada, the **loonie** (French: _huard_), formally the **one-dollar coin**, is a gold-coloured Canadian coin introduced in 1987 that is worth one dollar. Its purpose was to replace the country's one-dollar bill.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-:1-3) It is minted by the Royal Canadian Mint at its facility in Winnipeg. The most prevalent versions of the coin show a common loon, a bird found throughout most of Canada, on the reverse and Queen Elizabeth II, the nation's head of state at the time of the coin's issue, on the obverse. Various commemorative and specimen-set editions of the coin with special designs replacing the loon on the reverse have been minted over the years. Beginning in December 2023, a new version featuring King Charles III entered circulation.

The coin's outline is an 11-sidedReuleaux polygon. Its diameter of 26.5 mm (1.04 in) and its 11-sidedness match that of the already-circulating Susan B. Anthony dollar in the United States, and its thickness of 1.95 mm (0.077 in) is a close match to that coin's 2.0 mm (0.079 in) thickness. Its gold colour differs from the silver-coloured Anthony dollar; however, the succeeding Sacagawea and presidential dollars match the loonie's overall hue. Other coins using a non-circular curve of constant width include the 7-sided British twenty pence and fifty pence coins (the latter of which has similar size and value to the loonie but is silver in colour).
After its introduction, the coin became a metonym for the Canadian dollar: media often discuss the rate at which the loonie is trading against other currencies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-4) The nickname _loonie_ became so widely recognized that in 2006, the Royal Canadian Mint secured the rights to it.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-5) When the Canadian two-dollar coin was introduced in 1996, it was in turn nicknamed the "toonie" (a portmanteau of "two" and "loonie").

Canada first minted a silver dollar coin in 1935 to celebrate the 25th anniversary of George V's reign as king.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-6) The voyageur dollar, so named because it featured an Indigenous person and a French voyageur paddling a canoe on the reverse, was minted in silver until 1967, after which it was composed primarily of nickel.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-7) The coins did not see wide circulation, mainly due to their size and weight; the nickel version weighs 15.6 grams (0.55 oz) and is 32.1 millimetres (1.26 in) in diameter,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-EJDollarReplace-8) and is itself smaller than the silver version.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-9) By 1978, Canadian businesses, namely vending machine operators, and transit authorities were advocating for a one-dollar coin that circulated more easily.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10)
By 1982, the Royal Canadian Mint had begun work on a new composition for the dollar coin that it hoped would lead to increased circulation.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-EJDollarReplace-8) At the same time, vending machine operators and transit systems were lobbying the Government of Canada to replace the dollar banknotes with more widely circulating coins. A Commons committee recommended in 1985 that the dollar bill be eliminated despite a lack of evidence that Canadians would support the move.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-OC1985DollarCoin-11) The government argued that it would save between $175 million and $250 million over 20 years by switching from bills that had a lifespan of less than a year to coins that would last two decades.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CBCArchiveLoonie-12)

The government announced on March 25, 1986, that the new dollar coin would be launched the following year as a replacement for the dollar bill, which would be phased out.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-OCCoinIntroduced-13) Two proposals for the coin were considered, one by Inco for the Nigold coin, and one by Sheritt Gordon Mines for an aureate bronze plated on pure nickel (aureate nickel) coin. The government selected the Sherritt Gordon Mines proposal as it was less costly and the innovative technology behind the coin could serve to demonstrate the Royal Canadian Mint's capabilities in the international coinage market.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10)
It was expected to cost $31.8 million to produce the first 300 million coins but, through seigniorage (the difference between the cost of production and the coin's value), expected to make up to $40 million a year on the coins. From the proceeds, a total of $60 million over five years was dedicated toward funding the 1988 Winter Olympics in Calgary.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-14)
The failure of the Susan B. Anthony dollar coin in the United States had been considered and it was believed Americans refused to support the coin due to its similarity to their quarter coin and its lack of aesthetic appeal.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-OC1985DollarCoin-11) In announcing the new Canadian dollar coin, the government stated it would be the same overall size as the Susan B. Anthony coin – slightly larger than a quarter – to allow for compatibility with American manufactured vending machines but would be eleven-sided and gold-coloured.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-OCCoinIntroduced-13) The sample Canadian dollar was well received in test groups, with 80% of participants feeling its size, shape and colour made it more easily discernible from other coins.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10)

It was planned that the coin would continue using the _voyageur_ theme reverse designed by Emanuel Hahn and an obverse effigy of Queen Elizabeth II designed by Arnold Machine.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10) However, the master dies that had been struck in Ottawa were lost in transit en route to the Mint's facility at Winnipeg.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CTV20thAnniversary-15) A Commons committee struck to investigate the loss discovered that the Mint had no documented procedures for transport of master dies and that it had shipped them via a local courier in a bid to save $43.50. It was also found to be the third time that the Mint had lost master dies within five years.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-16) An internal review by the Royal Canadian Mint argued that while a policy existed to ship the obverse and reverse dies separately, the new coin dies were packaged separately but were part of the same shipment. The Mint also disagreed with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police's contention that the dies were simply lost in transit, believing instead that they were stolen.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-17) The dies were never recovered.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CTV20thAnniversary-15)

Fearing the possibility of counterfeiting, the government approved a new design for the reverse, replacing the _voyageur_ with a Robert-Ralph Carmichael design of a common loon floating in water.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CTV20thAnniversary-15) Carmichael's design had been submitted to the Royal Canadian Mint in 1978 and was chosen from the existing bank of designs maintained by the Mint.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10) In particular, the choice of the loon motif fit well with the other existing wildlife depictions used with the five-and twenty-five cent coins.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10) The Canadian Wildlife Federation provided strong approval of the design choice.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10)
The coin was immediately nicknamed the _loonie_ across English Canada and became known as a _huard_, French for 'loon', in Quebec.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CBCArchiveLoonie-12) The loonie entered circulation on June 30, 1987, as 40 million coins were introduced into major cities across the country.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-18) Over 800 million loonies had been struck by the coin's 20th anniversary.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-Ch20thAnniversary-19)

After a 21-month period in which the loonie and $1 note were produced concurrently with each other, the Bank of Canada ceased production of the dollar banknote. The final dollar bills were printed on June 30, 1989.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CHBillDemise-20) Initial support for the coin was mixed,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-21) but withdrawing the banknote forced acceptance of the coin.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-22)
The loonie has subsequently gained iconic status within Canada,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-Ch20thAnniversary-19) and is now regarded as a national symbol.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-Spec20th-23) The term "loonie" has since become synonymous with the Canadian dollar itself.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-24) The town of Echo Bay, Ontario, home of Robert-Ralph Carmichael, erected a large loonie monument in his honour in 1992 along the highway, similar to Sudbury's 'Big Nickel'.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-25)
A year after the death of Elizabeth II, a new loonie featuring the image of Charles III designed by Steven Rosati was revealed on November 14, 2023. A small number of the coins entered circulation in December 2023.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-26)

### **Striking in its Solitude – the 1‑dollar Coin, familiarly known as the 'loonie'**
The 1-dollar circulation coin was introduced in 1987 as a cost-saving measure to replace the one-dollar bill. The coin was instantly dubbed the 'loonie' after the solitary loon that graces the coin's reverse side. The nickname caught on and Canadians have been using it ever since. The loon design was created by noted wildlife artist Robert-Ralph Carmichael.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1935 – 1938, 1940 – 1948, 1950 – 1957, 1959 – 1963, 1965 – 1966, 1968 – 1969, and 1975 – 1986
The Voyageur
This design by Emanuel Hahn features a voyageur and his Indigenous guide travelling by canoe. The illustration has been modified only slightly over the years.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1939
The Royal Visit
This design by Emanuel Hahn commemorates the visit of His Majesty King George VI and Queen Elizabeth to Ottawa. The Latin phrase "Fide Quorum Regnat" means "He reigns by the faith of his people."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1949
Newfoundland joins Confederation
Thomas Shingles' design commemorates Newfoundland's status as a province of Canada. Pictured on the coin is the _Matthew_, the ship historians believe John Cabot was sailing when he landed in Newfoundland in 1497. Below the ship reads the Latin inscription "Floreat Terra Nova," meaning: "May the New Found Land Flourish."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1958
The founding of British Columbia
Stephen Trenka's representation of a mortuary pole with the Rocky Mountain backdrop marks the centenary of both the Cariboo Gold Rush and the creation of British Columbia as a colony of England.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1964
The Confederation meetings
Thomas Shingles' design features the French fleur-de-lis, the Irish shamrock, the Scottish thistle, and the English rose. It commemorates the 100th anniversary of the Charlottetown and Quebec City meetings that led to Confederation.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1967
The centennial dollar
Alex Colville created a special set of coin designs to commemorate the 100th anniversary of Canadian Confederation; the 1-dollar coin features a Canada goose.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1970
Manitoba's centennial
Raymond Taylor's prairie crocus design commemorates the centennial of Manitoba joining Confederation.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1971
British Columbia's centennial
Thomas Shingles' design commemorates the centennial of British Columbia's joining Confederation. The coin features British Columbia's coat of arms and its provincial flower, the dogwood.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1973
Prince Edward Island's centennial
Walter Ott's rendering of P.E.I.'s Provincial Legislature building commemorates the centennial of the province's accession to Canada.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1974
Winnipeg's centennial

In Canada, the **loonie** (French: _huard_), formally the **one-dollar coin**, is a gold-coloured Canadian coin introduced in 1987 that is worth one dollar. Its purpose was to replace the country's one-dollar bill.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-:1-3) It is minted by the Royal Canadian Mint at its facility in Winnipeg. The most prevalent versions of the coin show a common loon, a bird found throughout most of Canada, on the reverse and Queen Elizabeth II, the nation's head of state at the time of the coin's issue, on the obverse. Various commemorative and specimen-set editions of the coin with special designs replacing the loon on the reverse have been minted over the years. Beginning in December 2023, a new version featuring King Charles III entered circulation.
texts.1:
The coin's outline is an 11-sidedReuleaux polygon. Its diameter of 26.5 mm (1.04 in) and its 11-sidedness match that of the already-circulating Susan B. Anthony dollar in the United States, and its thickness of 1.95 mm (0.077 in) is a close match to that coin's 2.0 mm (0.079 in) thickness. Its gold colour differs from the silver-coloured Anthony dollar; however, the succeeding Sacagawea and presidential dollars match the loonie's overall hue. Other coins using a non-circular curve of constant width include the 7-sided British twenty pence and fifty pence coins (the latter of which has similar size and value to the loonie but is silver in colour).
After its introduction, the coin became a metonym for the Canadian dollar: media often discuss the rate at which the loonie is trading against other currencies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-4) The nickname _loonie_ became so widely recognized that in 2006, the Royal Canadian Mint secured the rights to it.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-5) When the Canadian two-dollar coin was introduced in 1996, it was in turn nicknamed the "toonie" (a portmanteau of "two" and "loonie").
texts.2:
Canada first minted a silver dollar coin in 1935 to celebrate the 25th anniversary of George V's reign as king.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-6) The voyageur dollar, so named because it featured an Indigenous person and a French voyageur paddling a canoe on the reverse, was minted in silver until 1967, after which it was composed primarily of nickel.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-7) The coins did not see wide circulation, mainly due to their size and weight; the nickel version weighs 15.6 grams (0.55 oz) and is 32.1 millimetres (1.26 in) in diameter,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-EJDollarReplace-8) and is itself smaller than the silver version.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-9) By 1978, Canadian businesses, namely vending machine operators, and transit authorities were advocating for a one-dollar coin that circulated more easily.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10)
By 1982, the Royal Canadian Mint had begun work on a new composition for the dollar coin that it hoped would lead to increased circulation.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-EJDollarReplace-8) At the same time, vending machine operators and transit systems were lobbying the Government of Canada to replace the dollar banknotes with more widely circulating coins. A Commons committee recommended in 1985 that the dollar bill be eliminated despite a lack of evidence that Canadians would support the move.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-OC1985DollarCoin-11) The government argued that it would save between $175 million and $250 million over 20 years by switching from bills that had a lifespan of less than a year to coins that would last two decades.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CBCArchiveLoonie-12)
texts.3:
The government announced on March 25, 1986, that the new dollar coin would be launched the following year as a replacement for the dollar bill, which would be phased out.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-OCCoinIntroduced-13) Two proposals for the coin were considered, one by Inco for the Nigold coin, and one by Sheritt Gordon Mines for an aureate bronze plated on pure nickel (aureate nickel) coin. The government selected the Sherritt Gordon Mines proposal as it was less costly and the innovative technology behind the coin could serve to demonstrate the Royal Canadian Mint's capabilities in the international coinage market.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10)
It was expected to cost $31.8 million to produce the first 300 million coins but, through seigniorage (the difference between the cost of production and the coin's value), expected to make up to $40 million a year on the coins. From the proceeds, a total of $60 million over five years was dedicated toward funding the 1988 Winter Olympics in Calgary.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-14)
The failure of the Susan B. Anthony dollar coin in the United States had been considered and it was believed Americans refused to support the coin due to its similarity to their quarter coin and its lack of aesthetic appeal.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-OC1985DollarCoin-11) In announcing the new Canadian dollar coin, the government stated it would be the same overall size as the Susan B. Anthony coin – slightly larger than a quarter – to allow for compatibility with American manufactured vending machines but would be eleven-sided and gold-coloured.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-OCCoinIntroduced-13) The sample Canadian dollar was well received in test groups, with 80% of participants feeling its size, shape and colour made it more easily discernible from other coins.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10)
texts.4: It was planned that the coin would continue using the _voyageur_ theme reverse designed by Emanuel Hahn and an obverse effigy of Queen Elizabeth II designed by Arnold Machine.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10) However, the master dies that had been struck in Ottawa were lost in transit en route to the Mint's facility at Winnipeg.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CTV20thAnniversary-15) A Commons committee struck to investigate the loss discovered that the Mint had no documented procedures for transport of master dies and that it had shipped them via a local courier in a bid to save $43.50. It was also found to be the third time that the Mint had lost master dies within five years.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-16) An internal review by the Royal Canadian Mint argued that while a policy existed to ship the obverse and reverse dies separately, the new coin dies were packaged separately but were part of the same shipment. The Mint also disagreed with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police's contention that the dies were simply lost in transit, believing instead that they were stolen.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-17) The dies were never recovered.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CTV20thAnniversary-15)
texts.5:
Fearing the possibility of counterfeiting, the government approved a new design for the reverse, replacing the _voyageur_ with a Robert-Ralph Carmichael design of a common loon floating in water.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CTV20thAnniversary-15) Carmichael's design had been submitted to the Royal Canadian Mint in 1978 and was chosen from the existing bank of designs maintained by the Mint.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10) In particular, the choice of the loon motif fit well with the other existing wildlife depictions used with the five-and twenty-five cent coins.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10) The Canadian Wildlife Federation provided strong approval of the design choice.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-SaSC-10)
The coin was immediately nicknamed the _loonie_ across English Canada and became known as a _huard_, French for 'loon', in Quebec.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CBCArchiveLoonie-12) The loonie entered circulation on June 30, 1987, as 40 million coins were introduced into major cities across the country.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-18) Over 800 million loonies had been struck by the coin's 20th anniversary.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-Ch20thAnniversary-19)
texts.6:
After a 21-month period in which the loonie and $1 note were produced concurrently with each other, the Bank of Canada ceased production of the dollar banknote. The final dollar bills were printed on June 30, 1989.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-CHBillDemise-20) Initial support for the coin was mixed,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-21) but withdrawing the banknote forced acceptance of the coin.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-22)
The loonie has subsequently gained iconic status within Canada,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-Ch20thAnniversary-19) and is now regarded as a national symbol.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-Spec20th-23) The term "loonie" has since become synonymous with the Canadian dollar itself.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-24) The town of Echo Bay, Ontario, home of Robert-Ralph Carmichael, erected a large loonie monument in his honour in 1992 along the highway, similar to Sudbury's 'Big Nickel'.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-25)
A year after the death of Elizabeth II, a new loonie featuring the image of Charles III designed by Steven Rosati was revealed on November 14, 2023. A small number of the coins entered circulation in December 2023.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loonie#cite_note-26)

The 1-dollar circulation coin was introduced in 1987 as a cost-saving measure to replace the one-dollar bill. The coin was instantly dubbed the 'loonie' after the solitary loon that graces the coin's reverse side. The nickname caught on and Canadians have been using it ever since. The loon design was created by noted wildlife artist Robert-Ralph Carmichael.
